## The instances

1. mimid-gn1w: `stock_rust_client_chats_through_two_daemons`. "no
   StateChange on the reconnecting stream in 15s; no frames arrived at
   all". Isolated: 2.75s. Under load: timed out at 15s.
2. mimid-h5c2: `a_call_in_a_chat_of_more_than_two_is_refused`. A call
   that should have been refused for having three participants was
   created, so the serving path saw a stale participant list.
3. `calls_across_two_providers` (crates/mimid-agent/tests/calls.rs).
   "no line from the server in time". Isolated: 3.4s, three times.
   Under load: failed after 35.5s.

## Why one bead

The common factor is not the code under test -- an SSE stream, a VTC
policy check and an IRC line have little to do with each other -- it is
that each waits on another task making progress, and under the full run
there are around 114 test binaries competing for 18 threads. A fix that
works for one probably works for all three, and three separate
"increase the timeout" patches would hide all three.

Instance 2 is the one that is not obviously only a test problem: a stale
participant read would be a real defect in a policy check, which is why
mimid-h5c2 is filed separately at P1 and stays open on its own terms.

   two places to start, since they are shared by many tests.

   wait was for, as mimid-gn1w's improved message now does -- that
   message is what told us "no frames arrived at all" and ruled out a

event and time out, and all three only fail under

   created, so the serving path saw a stale participant list.

   "no line from the server in time". Isolated: 3.4s, three times.
   Under load: failed after 35.5s.

## Why one bead

The common factor is not the code under test -- an SSE stream, a VTC
policy check and an IRC line have little to do with each other -- it is
that each waits on another task making progress, and under the full run
there are around 114 test binaries competing for 18 threads. A fix that
works for one probably works for all three, and three separate
"increase the timeout" patches would hide all three.

Instance 2 is the one that is not obviously only a test problem: a stale
participant read would be a real defect in a policy check, which is why
mimid-h5c2 is filed separately at P1 and stays open on its own terms.

## What to do, in order

1. Measure rather than guess: run the suite with
   `--test-threads` reduced and see whether the flakes stop. If they do,
   the waits are too short for the load, not wrong.
2. Prefer waiting on a condition over a fixed deadline where the test
   harness allows it. The helper at
   crates/mimid-agent/tests/common/irc.rs:118 and the SSE helper are the
   two places to start, since they are shared by many tests.
3. Only then consider longer deadlines, and say in the message what the
   wait was for, as mimid-gn1w's improved message now does -- that
   message is what told us "no frames arrived at all" and ruled out a
   publish/subscribe race.

Do not mark any of the three resolved on the strength of passing in
isolation. That is how all three got here.

## Two corrections to the above, 2026-11-26

**The waits are already condition-based.** All 37 uses of PATIENCE are
`timeout(PATIENCE, <await>)`, wrapping a read or a receive that
completes as soon as the thing arrives. The deadline is a failure
backstop, not a poll interval, so step 2 as written has nothing to act
on: there is no fixed deadline to replace with a condition. What is
fixed is the 15s wall clock, which does not scale with how loaded the
machine is.

**"114 binaries competing for 18 threads" needs checking.** cargo
runs test TARGETS one after another and parallelises the tests inside
each binary, so the competition is probably within a binary -- several
tests each starting servers and daemons -- not across binaries. The
number of test targets is not the right denominator, and the lever is
`--test-threads`.

So the revised plan:

1. Measure with `--test-threads=4` on an 18-core machine (18 cores
   confirmed by nproc) and compare against the default. A run is in
   progress.
2. If reduced threads removes the flakes, the cause is contention and
   the choice is between bounding parallelism in CI (slower for
   everyone) and making PATIENCE scale, for example from an env var the
   full-suite run sets, leaving the 15s default for isolated runs. The
   second keeps a real hang detectable, just later.
3. If reduced threads does NOT remove them, contention is not the cause
   and each flake needs its own diagnosis. mimid-h5c2 would then be
   much more likely to be the product bug it might be.

One run proves little either way: each of the three failed once across
roughly fifteen full-suite runs today. Treat a clean reduced-threads run
as weak evidence and keep the comparison going over later gates."}

   created, so the serving path saw a stale participant list.
3. `calls_across_two_providers` (crates/mimid-agent/tests/calls.rs).
   "no line from the server in time". Isolated: 3.4s, three times.
   Under load: failed after 35.5s.

## Why one bead

The common factor is not the code under test -- an SSE stream, a VTC
policy check and an IRC line have little to do with each other -- it is
that each waits on another task making progress, and under the full run

Instance 2 is the one that is not obviously only a test problem: a stale
participant read would be a real defect in a policy check, which is why

## What to do, in order

1. Measure rather than guess: run the suite with
   `--test-threads` reduced and see whether the flakes stop. If they do,
   the waits are too short for the load, not wrong.
2. Prefer waiting on a condition over a fixed deadline where the test

   crates/mimid-agent/tests/common/irc.rs:118 and the SSE helper are the
   two places to start, since they are shared by many tests.
3. Only then consider longer deadlines, and say in the message what the
   wait was for, as mimid-gn1w's improved message now does -- that
   message is what told us "no frames arrived at all" and ruled out a
   publish/subscribe race.

Do not mark any of the three resolved on the strength of passing in
isolation. That is how all three got here.

## Two corrections to the above, 2026-11-26

**The waits are already condition-based.** All 37 uses of PATIENCE are
`timeout(PATIENCE, <await>)`, wrapping a read or a receive that
completes as soon as the thing arrives. The deadline is a failure
backstop, not a poll interval, so step 2 as written has nothing to act
on: there is no fixed deadline to replace with a condition. What is
fixed is the 15s wall clock, which does not scale with how loaded the
machine is.

**"114 binaries competing for 18 threads" needs checking.** cargo
runs test TARGETS one after another and parallelises the tests inside
each binary, so the competition is probably within a binary -- several
tests each starting servers and daemons -- not across binaries. The
number of test targets is not the right denominator, and the lever is
`--test-threads`.

So the revised plan:

1. Measure with `--test-threads=4` on an 18-core machine (18 cores
   confirmed by nproc) and compare against the default. A run is in
   progress.
2. If reduced threads removes the flakes, the cause is contention and
   the choice is between bounding parallelism in CI (slower for
   everyone) and making PATIENCE scale, for example from an env var the
   full-suite run sets, leaving the 15s default for isolated runs. The
   second keeps a real hang detectable, just later.
3. If reduced threads does NOT remove them, contention is not the cause
   and each flake needs its own diagnosis. mimid-h5c2 would then be
   much more likely to be the product bug it might be.

One run proves little either way: each of the three failed once across
roughly fifteen full-suite runs today. Treat a clean reduced-threads run
as weak evidence and keep the comparison going over later gates.

## Measurement, 2026-11-26

`cargo test --workspace --all-features --no-fail-fast -- --test-threads=4`
on the 18-core machine: 2224 passed, 0 failed, exit 0. Same count as
the default-threads gate, so nothing was skipped.

That is ONE clean run, and it is weak evidence as the plan above says:
each flake failed once in roughly fifteen default-threads runs, so a
single clean run at a different setting distinguishes little. It does
not show that reduced threads fixes anything; it only fails to
contradict it.

## The group is now two flakes, not three

Bead mimid-h5c2 is diagnosed and does not belong here: its participant
list is OVERWRITTEN by a sync tick, not read late, so no deadline or
thread count affects it. Grouping all three under one trigger was
partly wrong.

What is left is two fixed-deadline timeouts, mimid-gn1w and
`calls_across_two_providers`, both at PATIENCE = 15s, both with a 5x
margin when run alone. For those the candidate fix is to let PATIENCE
scale for a full-suite run while leaving the 15s default for isolated
runs. A genuine hang still fails that way, just later -- gn1w's "no
frames arrived at all" would stay a failure however long the wait."}
